title: Medicine Across Cultures
bigQuestion: How can doctors and patients from different cultures understand and trust each other well enough to heal together?

story.title: The Grandmother in the Corner
story.kicker: A young doctor learns that the quietest person in the exam room may be the one who decides.
paragraphs: Dr. Kim has just finished her training at a Chicago hospital. Her patient is a 58-year-old man with diabetes whose blood sugar is climbing. She explains a new medicine to him and to his adult son, who translates. The man nods politely. In the corner of the room sits his mother, silent, holding her purse on her lap.

Two weeks later, the man returns. He has not taken the new medicine. Dr. Kim is puzzled. This time a trained interpreter joins the visit instead of the son. Dr. Kim asks the man what he thinks is causing his illness and what worries him about the medicine.

The answer surprises her. In this family, the grandmother makes the big health decisions. She worried that the pills were too strong. She had been giving her son a tea from their home country. No one had asked her opinion, so no one had answered her questions.

At the next visit, Dr. Kim speaks to the grandmother first, through the interpreter. She listens to her concerns and asks about the tea. She explains how the medicine works and checks that it is safe to use with the tea. The grandmother agrees. The man starts the medicine. Nothing about the science changed. What changed was the listening.
story.think: What did Dr. Kim do differently the second and third time? Which change do you think mattered most?

lessons.title: Culturally Responsive Care
lessons.mainIdea: Culturally responsive care means learning each patient's beliefs and needs and shaping care to fit them.
reading: In Dr. Kim's story, the medicine was right, but the plan failed at first. The family's way of making decisions was not part of the visit. Health workers call the fix *culturally responsive care*: care that respects a patient's culture, language and values and adjusts to them.

Culture includes language, religion, food, family roles and ideas about what causes illness. It does not decide what any one person believes. Two people from the same country may think very differently. Good clinicians avoid *stereotypes*, fixed ideas about a whole group, and instead ask each patient.

Psychiatrist and anthropologist Arthur Kleinman, at Harvard, suggested simple questions to learn a patient's *explanatory model*, their own view of the illness. What do you call this problem? What do you think caused it? What do you fear most? What kind of treatment do you hope for? These questions invite the patient to teach the doctor.

words.d: health care that learns and respects a patient's culture, language and values and adjusts to them
a fixed, oversimplified idea about everyone in a group
a person's own understanding of what an illness is, what caused it and how it should be treated

look.title: Asking About the Illness
look.text: Kleinman proposed that clinicians ask patients what they call their problem, what they think caused it, why it started when it did, what it does to them, how severe it is, what they fear, and what treatment they hope to receive.
look.cite: Arthur Kleinman, Leon Eisenberg and Byron Good, 'Culture, Illness, and Care,' Annals of Internal Medicine, 1978
look.prompt: Pick two of these questions. What might a doctor learn from each that a lab test could not show?

check.q: What is culturally responsive care?
choices: Care only for people from other countries
Care that learns and respects a patient's culture and adjusts to it
Care that uses only traditional remedies
Care given in one language only
check.why: Culturally responsive care adjusts to a patient's culture, language and values.

check.q: Why should clinicians avoid stereotypes?
choices: Culture has no effect on health
People from the same group can believe very different things
check.why: The reading says culture does not decide what any one person believes, so each patient must be asked.

check.q: Which question helps a doctor learn a patient's explanatory model?
choices: What do you think caused this problem?
check.why: Kleinman's questions ask about the patient's own view of the illness and its cause.

lessons.title: Working With Interpreters
lessons.mainIdea: Trained medical interpreters help patients and clinicians understand each other accurately and safely.
reading: In the story, the son translated at first. He loved his father, but he was not trained. He may have left out words, softened bad news, or felt shy about personal questions. A trained *medical interpreter* knows medical words in both languages and is taught to repeat everything accurately and privately.

In the United States, Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 bars discrimination based on national origin in programs that receive federal money. Federal agencies have long read this to mean that hospitals and clinics taking Medicare or Medicaid funds must offer language help to people with *limited English proficiency*. Many hospitals offer interpreters in person, by phone or by video.

Using children as interpreters is discouraged except in emergencies. A child may not know medical terms and should not have to deliver hard news to a parent. A good visit with an interpreter has the doctor speak to the patient, not to the interpreter, in short sentences, with time to ask questions.

words.d: a trained person who turns spoken words from one language into another accurately during health care
not yet speaking, reading or understanding English well enough for complex conversations
the part of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 that bars discrimination by national origin in federally funded programs

look.title: Two Visits
look.text: Visit A: A 12-year-old translates for her mother, who has a lump in her breast. The girl does not know the word 'biopsy' and looks scared. Visit B: A trained interpreter on a video screen repeats every word. The doctor looks at the mother and pauses often so she can ask questions.
look.prompt: List two risks in Visit A and two strengths in Visit B.

check.q: Why is a trained interpreter better than a family member in most visits?
choices: Family members are not allowed in hospitals
Trained interpreters know medical terms and repeat everything accurately
Interpreters make the decisions for patients
Family members always speak too slowly
check.why: Trained interpreters know medical words in both languages and are taught to be accurate and private.

check.q: Which law is linked to language help in federally funded health care?
choices: Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964
check.why: Title VI bars national-origin discrimination in programs that receive federal money.

check.q: In a good interpreted visit, whom should the doctor speak to?
check.why: The doctor speaks directly to the patient, and the interpreter repeats the words.

lessons.title: Listening as a Medical Skill
lessons.mainIdea: Careful listening is a medical skill that helps clinicians find the problem and helps patients follow the plan.
reading: Researchers who have recorded doctor visits found that doctors often interrupt patients within the first minute of the visit. When patients are allowed to finish their opening story, most take only a minute or two. What they say often holds the key to the problem.

A saying often credited to the Canadian physician William Osler, who taught around 1900, advises doctors to listen to the patient, because the patient is telling you the diagnosis. Whether or not Osler said it in those words, the idea is widely taught in medical schools today.

One practical tool is *teach-back*. After explaining a plan, the clinician asks the patient to explain it back in their own words: 'So I know I explained it well, can you tell me how you will take this medicine?' If something is unclear, the clinician explains again. Teach-back checks the clinician's teaching, not the patient's intelligence.

words.d: a method where the patient explains the plan back in their own words to check understanding
the identification of an illness or problem from its signs and symptoms
listening with full attention, without interrupting, and checking that you understood

look.title: Try Teach-Back
look.text: A nurse explains: 'Take one pill each morning with food, and call us if you feel dizzy.' Then she says, 'I want to make sure I explained that clearly. Can you tell me how you'll take it?' The patient answers, 'One pill at night.' The nurse smiles and explains again.
look.prompt: What did teach-back catch here? Why does the nurse say 'I want to make sure I explained that clearly' instead of 'Did you understand?'

check.q: What is teach-back?
choices: A test given to patients in school
The patient explaining the plan back in their own words
check.why: In teach-back, the patient explains the plan back so the clinician can check the explanation.

check.q: What did researchers who recorded visits find?
choices: Doctors often interrupt within the first minute
check.why: Studies found early interruptions, even though patients' full stories are usually short.

check.q: Why does the reading say to be careful about the Osler saying?
choices: It may not be his exact words
check.why: The reading says the saying is 'often credited' to Osler, so the exact words are uncertain.

lessons.title: Who Makes the Decision?
lessons.mainIdea: In many cultures, health decisions are made by the family together, and good care makes room for that.
reading: U.S. medical ethics puts strong weight on *autonomy*, the right of each adult patient to make their own choices. In many families, though, decisions are shared. In many Asian and Latin American families, for example, parents, grown children or elders often take part. A patient may want the family to hear bad news first.

In many Latino families, *familismo* describes strong loyalty and closeness within the family, including in health choices. In many East Asian families, adult children may be expected to guide care for aging parents. These are patterns, not rules. Each family, and each person, is different.

Clinicians can respect both autonomy and family by asking the patient directly: 'Do you want to hear the results yourself, or would you like me to talk with someone in your family?' The patient's own answer then guides the plan. This honors their choice, even when the choice is to share the decision.

words.d: a person's right to make their own choices about their body and care
a value in many Latino cultures that puts strong loyalty and closeness within the family
choosing a treatment together, with the patient, family and clinician all taking part

look.title: One Question First
look.text: Mrs. Chen, 80, has test results back. Her daughter asks the doctor to tell her the news first, in the hallway. The doctor steps into the room, sits down, and asks Mrs. Chen through an interpreter how she would like to hear her results and who should be with her.
look.prompt: Why did the doctor ask Mrs. Chen instead of simply agreeing with the daughter or refusing her?

check.q: What does autonomy mean in medical ethics?
choices: A patient's right to make their own choices
check.why: Autonomy is each adult patient's right to make their own decisions.

check.q: How can a clinician respect both autonomy and family?
choices: Ask the patient how they want decisions made
Let the oldest relative decide without asking
check.why: Asking the patient lets their own choice guide how the family takes part.

check.q: What does the reading say about cultural patterns such as familismo?
choices: They apply to everyone in a group
They are patterns, and each family is different
check.why: The reading stresses these are patterns, not rules; each family differs.

lessons.title: The Spirit Catches You
lessons.mainIdea: Anne Fadiman's book about a Hmong family and their doctors shows how misunderstanding can harm care even when everyone means well.
reading: In 1997, journalist Anne Fadiman published *The Spirit Catches You and You Fall Down*. It tells the true story of Lia Lee, a Hmong girl born in 1982 in Merced, California. Her family had come to the U.S. as refugees from Laos. As a baby, Lia began having serious seizures. Her doctors diagnosed *epilepsy*.

The book's title comes from a Hmong phrase for Lia's condition. In the family's view, the seizures involved her spirit, and they could even be a sign of special spiritual gifts. The doctors prescribed a complex, changing schedule of medicines. Without trained interpreters or shared understanding, the family often gave the medicines differently than prescribed, and both sides grew frustrated.

Fadiman showed that the parents loved Lia deeply and that the doctors worked hard to help her. The problem was not a lack of care but a lack of understanding. The book won the National Book Critics Circle Award and is still read in many medical schools. It helped spread the practice of asking about patients' beliefs.

words.d: a people from the mountains of Laos and nearby lands, many of whom came to the U.S. as refugees after the Vietnam War
a brain condition that causes repeated seizures
a person who has fled their country to escape war or danger

look.title: Two Views of One Illness
look.text: Fadiman wrote that she came to believe Lia's life might have gone differently if her doctors had asked the family what they believed and worked with them, and if the family had understood the doctors' reasons. She did not blame either side.
look.cite: Anne Fadiman, The Spirit Catches You and You Fall Down, 1997
look.prompt: Why do you think Fadiman chose not to blame either the family or the doctors? What does that teach future health workers?

check.q: Who wrote The Spirit Catches You and You Fall Down?
check.why: Journalist Anne Fadiman wrote the book, published in 1997.

check.q: What condition did Lia Lee's doctors diagnose?
check.why: Lia had serious seizures, and her doctors diagnosed epilepsy.

check.q: According to Fadiman, what was the main problem in Lia's care?
choices: The parents did not love her
A lack of understanding between the family and doctors
check.why: The book shows both sides cared, but they did not understand each other.

lessons.title: Working With Traditional Healers
lessons.mainIdea: The WHO encourages countries to bring safe, proven traditional medicine into health systems while protecting patients.
reading: In many parts of Africa and Asia, the first person a sick family visits is a traditional healer or herbalist. The World Health Organization notes that for many people, traditional medicine is the most available or trusted care. Ignoring it does not make it go away.

The WHO wrote a *Traditional Medicine Strategy* for 2014 to 2023. It urged countries to study traditional practices, regulate products and practitioners for safety, and include proven practices in health systems. In 2022, India and the WHO agreed to set up a WHO Global Centre for Traditional Medicine in Jamnagar, India.

Some programs train traditional healers to spot danger signs and send patients to clinics. In several African countries, healers have been trained to refer people for HIV testing. For patients, the key step is simple: tell your doctor, nurse or pharmacist about any herbs, teas or supplements you use, because some can change how medicines work.

words.d: a person who treats illness using the knowledge and practices of a culture's healing tradition
a WHO plan for 2014-2023 to make traditional medicine safer and better studied
sending a patient to another health worker or place for care

look.title: The WHO's Goals
look.text: The WHO strategy aimed to help countries use the potential of traditional and complementary medicine for health and well-being, and to promote its safe and effective use through regulation, research and bringing proven products and practitioners into health systems.
look.cite: World Health Organization, WHO Traditional Medicine Strategy 2014-2023, 2013
look.prompt: The strategy says 'safe and effective.' Why do you think both words are needed?

check.q: What did the WHO Traditional Medicine Strategy urge countries to do?
choices: Study, regulate and include proven practices
check.why: The strategy called for research, regulation for safety, and including proven practices.

check.q: Where is the WHO Global Centre for Traditional Medicine being set up?
check.why: India and the WHO agreed in 2022 to set up the centre in Jamnagar.

check.q: What is the key step for a patient who uses herbs or supplements?
choices: Tell a doctor, nurse or pharmacist
check.why: Some herbs change how medicines work, so clinicians need to know.

lessons.title: Why Some People Distrust Medicine
lessons.mainIdea: Past harms by medical researchers help explain why some communities are slow to trust health care today.
reading: From 1932 to 1972, the U.S. Public Health Service ran a study in Macon County, Alabama. It followed about 600 Black men, around 400 of whom had syphilis. The men were not told the truth about their illness. Even after penicillin became the standard cure in the 1940s, they were not offered it.

A news story in 1972 ended the study. In 1997, President Bill Clinton formally apologized on behalf of the nation. The study, often called the *Tuskegee syphilis study*, led to stronger rules protecting research volunteers, including *informed consent*: people must be told the truth and agree freely before taking part.

Researchers have found that memory of such harms, along with unfair treatment people meet today, can lower *trust* in medicine. Trust grows slowly. It grows when clinicians listen, explain honestly, respect a patient's choices, and when communities see people like themselves working in health care.

words.d: a 1932-1972 U.S. study in which Black men with syphilis were deceived and not treated
agreeing to care or research after being told the truth about its purpose, risks and choices
a belief that someone is honest and will act in your interest

look.title: Building Trust
look.text: A community clinic on Chicago's South Side hires health workers who grew up in the neighborhood. They hold health talks at churches and barbershops. They explain vaccines plainly and take questions without rushing. Over two years, more families come in for checkups.
look.prompt: Which actions in this scene connect to the reading's ideas about how trust grows?

check.q: What happened in the Tuskegee syphilis study?
choices: Men were deceived and not offered treatment
Men were cured quickly with penicillin
Doctors tested a new vaccine with consent
check.why: The men were not told the truth and were not offered penicillin even after it became the standard cure.

check.q: Which protection grew stronger because of this study?
check.why: The study led to stronger research rules, including informed consent.

check.q: According to the reading, what helps trust grow?
choices: Honest explanations and respect for patients' choices
check.why: Trust grows when clinicians listen, explain honestly and respect choices.

lessons.title: Health Disparities
lessons.mainIdea: Health disparities are gaps in health between groups, and they come from many causes that people can work to change.
reading: Two babies are born on the same day in the same city, a few miles apart. On average, one may live years longer than the other. Researchers have mapped these gaps by neighborhood in Chicago and in many U.S. cities. Such gaps between groups are called *health disparities*.

Disparities come from many sources. The *social determinants of health* are the conditions where people are born, live, learn, work and age: income, housing, safe streets, healthy food, schools and access to care. Unequal treatment and lack of insurance add to the gaps.

One well-measured example is maternal death. The CDC's National Center for Health Statistics reported that in 2021, Black women in the U.S. died from pregnancy-related causes at about 2.6 times the rate of white women. Many of these deaths are judged preventable. Hospitals and states are responding with safety checklists, better follow-up after birth and listening closely when patients report symptoms.

words.d: a gap in health or health care between groups of people
the conditions where people live, learn, work and age that shape their health
the death of a woman during pregnancy or soon after, from causes related to it

look.title: U.S. Maternal Death Rates, 2021
look.cite: Hoyert, CDC National Center for Health Statistics, Maternal Mortality Rates in the United States, 2021 (2023)
look.prompt: Compare the rates. Which social determinants of health might help explain the gap?

check.q: What is a health disparity?
choices: A gap in health between groups
check.why: A health disparity is a gap in health or care between groups of people.

check.q: Which is a social determinant of health?
choices: The brand of a hospital bed
check.why: Housing is one of the conditions where people live that shape health.

check.q: What did the CDC report about maternal deaths in 2021?
choices: Rates were equal for all groups
White women had the highest rate
Black women died at about 2.6 times the rate of white women
check.why: The CDC reported a Black maternal death rate about 2.6 times the white rate.

lessons.title: A Health Workforce for Everyone
lessons.mainIdea: Community health workers, diverse clinicians and patient voices help health systems serve every culture well.
reading: In many countries, *community health workers* link families and clinics. They are often trusted members of the neighborhood, trained to teach, check blood pressure, help people keep appointments and speak the local language. Studies show they can help people manage conditions like high blood pressure and diabetes.

Researchers have also studied *patient-clinician concordance*, meaning a patient and clinician share a language, background or experience. Some studies find that shared language improves understanding and satisfaction. The evidence on other kinds of shared background is mixed and still being studied.

Every health worker can build *cultural humility*. It means staying curious, admitting what you do not know, and learning from each patient for a whole career. It is less about memorizing facts about groups and more about asking good questions, listening, and adjusting care to the person in front of you.

words.d: a trusted local person trained to link neighbors with health care and teach healthy habits
when a patient and clinician share a language, background or experience
a lifelong habit of curiosity, admitting what you do not know and learning from each patient

look.title: Two Approaches
look.text: Student A memorizes a list: 'Group X believes this; Group Y eats that.' Student B practices asking every patient, 'What matters most to you about your health? What do you think is going on?' Both want to serve patients from many cultures.
look.prompt: Which student shows cultural humility? What risk might Student A's list create?

check.q: What do community health workers do?
choices: Link neighbors with care and teach healthy habits
check.why: Community health workers are trusted locals who link families with care.

check.q: What does the reading say about evidence on patient-clinician concordance?
choices: It has been proven for every kind of background
It shows no effect at all
Shared language helps; other evidence is mixed
check.why: The reading says shared language helps, while evidence on other shared backgrounds is mixed.

check.q: What is cultural humility?
choices: Staying curious and learning from each patient
check.why: Cultural humility is a lifelong habit of curiosity and learning from each person.

choices: A patient's own view of their illness and its cause
review.why: Kleinman's term describes how a patient understands the illness.

review.q: Why are trained interpreters preferred over children in most visits?
choices: It is always illegal for children to translate
Interpreters know medical terms and children should not carry hard news
review.why: Trained interpreters are accurate, and children should not deliver hard news to parents.

review.q: In Dr. Kim's story, what changed the patient's choice?
choices: Listening to the grandmother through an interpreter
review.why: The science stayed the same; listening to the decision-maker changed the outcome.

review.q: The Spirit Catches You and You Fall Down tells the story of which family?
review.why: Fadiman's book follows Lia Lee's Hmong family in Merced, California.

review.q: How does the WHO approach traditional medicine?
choices: It says all traditional remedies are proven
It urges research, regulation and including proven practices
review.why: The WHO Traditional Medicine Strategy calls for study, safety rules and integration of what is proven.

review.q: Which study helps explain mistrust of medicine in some Black communities?
review.why: The 1932-1972 Tuskegee study deceived Black men and withheld treatment.

review.q: What are social determinants of health?
choices: Conditions where people live, learn, work and age
review.why: They are the conditions, like housing and income, that shape health.

review.q: Which approach best shows cultural humility?
choices: Asking each patient what matters to them
Using one stereotype for each group
review.why: Cultural humility means asking, listening and learning from each person.
